sections.html:
Quincy, in Norfolk County just south of Boston, counted 101,636 residents in 2020 and 51,156 housing units. Commuters like the four Red Line stops (North Quincy, Wollaston, Quincy Center and Quincy Adams) plus Interstate 93 and Route 3.

Neighborhoods vary a lot. Squantum, Houghs Neck and Adams Shore are coastal and mostly peninsular, and began as summer communities before turning into year-round homes. Wollaston and North Quincy are dense and sit on the Red Line. Quincy Center holds City Hall and the historic core. Buyers eyeing an older waterside house tend to question the furnace, roof and basement.

Quincy divides the job. One office decides value, and the other collects.

The Assessors' Office sets values on roughly 27,000 parcels of every type, from homes to utilities. Abatement and exemption requests land on its desk. It stands behind its values when they are challenged at the state tax appeals board, and every sale in the city gets reported by it to the state revenue department. Visit 1305 Hancock Street, 1st Floor, or call (617) 376-1170, weekdays 8:30 AM to 4:30 PM.

Each year's rate grows out of a budget the Mayor and City Council set. A classification hearing in the Council Chamber comes first, then the council votes the rates, and the Assessors hand the total to the Treasurer-Collector. A disputed bill means two separate calls: the Assessors for value, the collector for payment.

Four installments fall due each fiscal year: August 1, November 1, February 1 and May 1.

Bills one and two are estimates. Added together they come to about half of last year's tax, divided into two equal payments. Bills three and four use the new assessed value and new rate and credit what you paid. Your new value first appears on the third bill, mailed in January.

BillDue dateWhat it reflects
Quarter 1August 1Preliminary, half of the prior-year total split in two
Quarter 2November 1Preliminary, second half of that amount
Quarter 3February 1Actual bill with new value and rate
Quarter 4May 1Final installment of the actual bill

Timing affects a sale. A house listed in early spring has three of the year's bills in play, and the payoff at closing depends on which have been paid.

Quincy's residential rate for fiscal year 2026 is $11.78 per $1,000 of assessed value. The commercial rate is $23.53 per $1,000. The city's tax rates page keeps the history:

  • Fiscal 2024: $11.27 residential, $22.45 commercial
  • Fiscal 2025: $11.53 residential, $23.01 commercial
  • Fiscal 2026: $11.78 residential, $23.53 commercial

For a rough estimate, multiply assessed value by the rate, divide by 1,000 and subtract any exemption. The bill itself is what counts.

An appeal begins with an abatement application to the Assessors. The usual deadline in a quarterly-billing city is February 1.

The Massachusetts Appellate Tax Board explains each step in its guide to real estate tax appeals. Here is the sequence.

  • Keep paying on schedule. Paying on time is a jurisdictional requirement, with narrow exceptions such as a tax of $5,000 or less.
  • Submit the approved abatement form by the date the actual bill's first installment is due.
  • The Assessors get three months. Inaction for three calendar months is treated as a denial.
  • Still unhappy? You have three months from their decision, or from the deemed denial, to file at the Appellate Tax Board.

The board starts by presuming the assessment is right, so you must show the fair cash value is lower. Comparable recent sales nearby, in similar condition, do that best. A tax increase on its own proves nothing.

Several groups qualify for statutory exemptions in Quincy, and you reapply each year. For fiscal year 2027 the filing deadline is April 1, 2027.

  • Senior citizens, with separate applications for ages 65 and up and ages 70 and up
  • Legally blind residents
  • Surviving spouses, and minor children of a deceased parent
  • Surviving spouses or minor children of police officers and firefighters
  • Disabled former service members, including anyone with a service-related disability of at least 10 percent

At minimum, you must be domiciled in Quincy. The Assessors also publish a tax deferral explanation for owners who qualify. Forms and details are on the exemption programs page.

Selling after a health change or a death in the family? Ask the Assessors whether an exemption you hold alters the final bill and the payoff.

sections.h2: If Quincy property tax goes unpaid
sections.html:
A lien attaches automatically when property tax goes unpaid. In time the city may record a taking, and a private holder may pursue foreclosure in Land Court. The court's foreclosure overview shows the usual path.

  1. After 30 days of nonpayment on a tax or water and sewer bill, a demand can be mailed to your last known address.
  2. If 14 more days pass without payment, a tax taking can be recorded at the Registry of Deeds.
  3. The tax title may end up with a private party, for instance after a bundled sale or an auction.
  4. Six or twelve months after the taking or sale, depending on the date, the holder may file a Land Court complaint.
  5. You may respond, request a hearing, and redeem by paying all taxes, interest and fees before a final judgment of foreclosure.

You can redeem right up until the court enters judgment. Many owners in arrears sell for that reason: the closing pays off the lien, and any equity left is yours.

A Quincy sale brings a deed excise tax, a smoke and carbon monoxide certificate, and payoff of any tax owed.

  • The Norfolk County Registry of Deeds charges a deed excise tax of $2.28 per $500 of the stated consideration. Its fee schedule also lists a $156 recording fee for a deed in recorded land.
  • A one or two family home needs a certificate of compliance from the local fire department showing that smoke and carbon monoxide alarms meet state requirements. The state's guidance says to call the fire department as soon as you have a closing date.
  • Ask both the Assessors and the Treasurer-Collector for the current balance, because the closing agent needs an exact payoff.
  • Bring your deed information and latest bill when you call, so the offices can find the parcel quickly.

A cash sale to Cash Home Buyers still needs these same items, but it skips the lender appraisal and the repair negotiations that often follow one. We buy houses as-is, so the alarm certificate is the main inspection task left, and the tax payoff is handled through closing.

faqs.q: How often is Quincy property tax billed?
faqs.a: Quarterly, due August 1, November 1, February 1 and May 1. The first two bills are preliminary and total about half of the prior year's tax.

faqs.q: What is Quincy's residential tax rate?
faqs.a: For fiscal year 2026 it is $11.78 per $1,000 of assessed value. The commercial rate is $23.53 per $1,000.

faqs.q: Can I sell my Quincy house if I owe back property tax?
faqs.a: Yes. Unpaid tax is a lien on the property, and the sale can pay it from the proceeds at closing. Get a written payoff figure from the city before the closing date.

faqs.q: What is the deadline for a Quincy property tax exemption?
faqs.a: Applications for fiscal year 2027 are due on or before April 1, 2027, and you must file again every year. You must be domiciled in Quincy.

faqs.q: How long do I have to challenge my Quincy assessment?
faqs.a: The abatement application is generally due February 1. After the Assessors act, you have three months to appeal to the Appellate Tax Board.
